preamble: Unrounding of the rounded vowel /œ/ to [ə], merging it with schwa. Afrikaans has a short rounded /œ/ (krul, bus, brug /brœχ/) whose unrounded counterpart is the central /ə/ of wind and hitte (Wissing 2020, The rounded and unrounded mid-central vowels); Swanepoel (1927) wrote that it "has no exact unrounded equivalent, but both [ɛ] and [ə], especially the latter, serve this purpose". He already called "the spreading of the rounded vowel" (krul > [krəl], skuld > [skəlt]) the most serious mistake of both English and Afrikaans speakers, warned that the rounded vowel was in grave danger of disappearing from Afrikaans, and listed the word pairs that would then fall together (kul – kil, stuk – stik, sug – sig, rug – rig, put – pit). Wissing (1994), citing Ponelis (1990/1), notes eighteenth-century spellings such as brig for brug and hilp for hulp, which show that derounding of the short rounded vowel is old. In his experiment, pooled over five rounded–unrounded pairs of which only dus – dis has /œ/, one speaker made no durational difference between the intended rounded and unrounded vowels and listeners recognised 49% of the intended rounded vowels as rounded; he reports large-scale derounding in everyday spoken Afrikaans, even in a radio sermon. In Wissing (2020, Vowel derounding) derounding differs by age: older speakers, especially those aged 70 and over, deround less than young speakers, and only three of twelve students in one test made a clear distinction between /ə/ and /œ/. He reads a discrimination task over the rounded vowels as pointing to two chronolects, which could also reflect a diachronic shift, while absolute neutralization of the contrast has not yet taken place. Derounding is favoured by fast speech and lack of stress but is not limited to them. Because the sources keep /œ/ and /ə/ apart as phonemes (dus – dis is a minimal pair) and record speakers who still contrast them, this is a merger in progress, not two transcriptions of one vowel. Phonetically Afrikaans /œ/ is a weakly rounded central vowel ([ɞ̝] or [ɞ]), and Wissing (1994) calls the term ontronding 'derounding' "eintlik onvanpas" ('actually unsuitable') because even the intended rounded vowels have little lip rounding; the atlas keeps the symbol œ used by all the sources.

examples.note: Swanepoel (1927: 38–39) gives krul [krœl] as an example of the rounded vowel and [krəl] as its unrounded pronunciation by both Afrikaans and English speakers.
Listed by Swanepoel (1927: 39) among the words in which the rounded vowel is spread (unrounded).
One of the stimulus words for /œ/ (with uur for /y/ and neus for /ø/) in Wissing and Van Dijkhorst (2006), as reported by Wissing (2020, Vowel derounding); derounding turned its vowel into [ə].
